```{r}
#| label: load-data
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| results: hide

source(here::here("0-config.R"))
source(here::here("analysis", "0-functions.R"))

df_all <- readRDS(here("data","grappe_mortality_data.rds"))

districts <- df_all %>% distinct(district) %>% pull(district)
grappes <- df_all %>% distinct(grappe) %>% pull(grappe)

df_proj <- df_all %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  st_as_sf(coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = global_crs) %>%
  st_transform(crs = proj_crs) %>%
  mutate(lon = sf::st_coordinates(.)[,1],
         lat = sf::st_coordinates(.)[,2])

dist_summ <- readRDS(here("data", "district_mortality_means.rds")) %>%
  filter(district %in% districts)

ate_preds <- readRDS(here("data", "preds_ATE.rds")) 
post_prob_raw <- readRDS(here("data", "post_prob_dat.rds"))

aics <- readRDS(here("data", "model_aic_table.rds"))
lrts <- readRDS(here("data", "model_lrt_table.rds"))

csi_preds <- readRDS(here("data", "csi_preds_mort.rds"))

niger_adm1 <- st_read(dsn = here("data", "untouched", "ner_admin_boundaries", "ner_admin1.shp"))
niger_adm2 <- st_read(dsn = here("data", "untouched", "ner_admin_boundaries", "ner_admin2.shp"))

niger_adm2_sub <- readRDS(here("data", "niger_adm2_sub.rds"))
niger_adm2_sub_proj <- niger_adm2_sub %>%
  st_transform(crs = proj_crs)
```

# Trial data and outcomes

## Histograms of person-time and mortality outcomes

### Overall distributions across all grappes

```{r}
#| label: histograms-overall

#| fig-height: 5

hist1 <- ggplot(data = df_all) +
  geom_histogram(aes(x = pt_year_1to59), bins = 30, fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
  labs(x = "Person-years of follow-up", y = "Number of grappes") +
  theme_minimal() +
  ylim(c(0, 350))

hist2 <- ggplot(data = df_all) +
  geom_histogram(aes(x = n_deaths_1to59), bins = 30, fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
  labs(x = "Number of deaths (1-59 months)", y = "Number of grappes") +
  theme_minimal() +
  ylim(c(0, 350)) +
  theme(axis.title.y = element_blank(),
        axis.text.y = element_blank())

hist3 <- ggplot(data = df_all) +
  geom_histogram(aes(x = deaths_per_1000_1to59), bins = 30, fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
  labs(x = "Mortality rate (deaths per 1000 py)", y = "Number of grappes") +
  theme_minimal() +
  ylim(c(0, 350)) +
  theme(axis.title.y = element_blank(),
        axis.text.y = element_blank())

hist1 | hist2 | hist3 
```

## Relationships between mortality outcomes and person-time, by treatment group

```{r}
#| label: par-coords-plot
#| fig-width: 8

par_coords_dat <- df_all %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  dplyr::select(isTreated_child, pt_year_1to59, n_deaths_1to59, deaths_per_1000_1to59) %>%
  mutate(row_n = row_number()) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = c(deaths_per_1000_1to59, n_deaths_1to59), 
               names_to = "variable", values_to = "value") %>%
   mutate(variable = factor(variable, levels = c("n_deaths_1to59", "deaths_per_1000_1to59"),
                            labels = c("# deaths", "deaths per 1000 py")))

mort_par <- ggplot(data = par_coords_dat) +
  geom_point(aes(x = variable, y = value, color = pt_year_1to59), alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_line(aes(x = variable, y = value, group = row_n, color = pt_year_1to59), alpha = 0.5) +
  facet_wrap(~isTreated_child, nrow = 2) +
  scale_color_viridis_c(name = "Person-years", option = "D", direction = -1, limits = c(0, 800)) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
        axis.title.x = element_blank())

mort_dot <- ggplot(data = df_all, aes(x = n_deaths_1to59, y = deaths_per_1000_1to59)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = pt_year_1to59), alpha = 0.5) +
  scale_color_viridis_c(name = "Person-years", option = "D", direction = -1, limits = c(0, 800)) +
  facet_wrap(~isTreated_child, nrow = 2) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  labs(x = "Total deaths", y = "Deaths per 1000 person-years") +

           label.x = 30, label.y = 10, hjust = 1, vjust = 0,

mort_par | mort_dot +

```

### Test of heterogeneity in mortality rates across departments

```{r}
#| label: heterogeneity-test

global_poi_mod <- glm(n_deaths_1to59 ~ isTreated_child + offset(log(pt_year_1to59)),
                      data = subset(df_all, pt_year_1to59 > 0), family = poisson(link = "log"))

state_poi_mod <- glm(n_deaths_1to59 ~ isTreated_child + factor(district) + offset(log(pt_year_1to59)),
                      data = subset(df_all, pt_year_1to59 > 0), family = poisson(link = "log"))

lmtest::lrtest(state_poi_mod, global_poi_mod)

```

### Table of ATE estimates by department

```{r table department effects}
#| label: department-ate-table

dist_summ %>%
  arrange(ATE) %>%
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)

```

Mortality rates are in deaths per 1000 person-years among children aged 1-59 months. ATE = mean mortality rate in treatment group - mean mortality rate in control group, by department. Negative ATEs are favorable.

The ATE estimates vary meaningfully across departments, with most showing reductions in mortality under treatment. The magnitude of the effect ranges, indicating heterogeneity in intervention effectiveness. Notably, Boboye is the only department with a positive ATE, which warrants further investigation.

### Boboye's positive ATE

Boboye is the only department with a positive ATE (higher mortality in treatment than control), so we look more closely at the spatial distribution of outcomes within that department.

  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  annotation_scale() +
  scale_x_continuous(name = "Longitude") +
  scale_y_continuous(name = "Latitude") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
        legend.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA),
        legend.title = element_text(hjust = 1, vjust = 0.5),

```{r}

#| fig.width: 7
#| fig.height: 5

boboye_long <- boboye_df %>%
  dplyr::select(isTreated_child, grappe, pt_year_1to59, n_deaths_1to59, deaths_per_1000_1to59) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = c(pt_year_1to59, n_deaths_1to59, deaths_per_1000_1to59), names_to = "variable", values_to = "value")

ggplot(data = boboye_long, aes(y = isTreated_child, x = value, color = isTreated_child)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(y = "Treatment group", title = "Boboye") +
  facet_wrap(~variable, scales = "free_x", ncol = 1) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")+
  scale_color_manual(breaks = c("Control", "Treatment"),
                     values = c("#fecd6c", "#e84d60"),
                     name = "Treatment Arm") 

```

The positive ATE does not seem to be driven by a few outliers with high mortality in the treatment group, but rather a general shift in the distribution of mortality rates across the department. Boboye also has the lowest overall mortality rates in the control arm and was also part of MORDOR and hence given MDA for an extended period of time, which may be related to the positive ATE.

# Spatial models

We fit four Poisson generalized linear mixed models accounting for spatial correlation through a Matérn-structured random effect to predict mortality rates across the study area. The models are:

1.  *Simple kriging model*: Has a Matern correlation structure and a binary treatment indicator and no covariates (simp_krig)
2.  *Generalized (Universal) kriging model*: Has a Matern correlation structure, a binary treatment indicator, and linear terms for latitude and longitude as covariates (gen_krig)
3.  *Generalized kriging model with interaction between treatment indicator and lat/lon terms*: Has a Matern correlation structure, a binary treatment indicator, linear terms for latitude and longitude as covariates, and an interaction between the treatment indicator and the linear lat/lon terms (gen_krig_int)
4.  *Generalized kriging model with a site-specific random effect*: Has a Matern correlation structure, a binary treatment indicator, linear terms for latitude and longitude as covariates, and a random effect term for grappe (gen_krig_re)

All models included an offset for log person-years of follow-up and were fit using the `spaMM::fitme()` function. We then used the fitted models to predict mortality rates across a grid of locations covering the study area and compared the predictions across models and treatment groups. We also used the predicted mortality rates to estimate the ATE across the study area and compared the spatial distribution of ATE estimates across models.

## Model comparison

```{r}
#| label: model-comparison

aics %>%
  arrange(AIC) %>%
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)

lrts %>%
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)

```

## Matern correlations

![](images/matern_corrs-2.png)

From the above correlation plots, we see that the simple kriging model has a much longer range and slower decay than the generalized kriging models. This is likely because the larger spatial range in the simple kriging model is trying to account for spatial variation that could be explained by the lat/lon covariates in the generalized kriging models. Based on a LRT and AIC values, the generalized kriging models all outperformed the simple kriging model.

Based on LRT and AIC values, the generalized kriging model with interaction was preferred. The similarity in correlation structures across the generalized models suggests that adding interaction terms or random effects does not substantially change the scale of spatial dependence, but instead refines how spatial variation is partitioned between fixed effects and residual spatial structure.

*NOTE* The "range" in these plots is just the inverse of the rho parameter in the matern correlation. We could use alternative definitions of range that might be more interpretable, such as the distance at which correlation drops to 0.1, for example.

## Mortality predictions from spatial models

```{r}
#| label: model-predictions
#| fig.height: 8
#| fig.width: 10

pred_long <- ate_preds %>%
  dplyr::select(-ATE) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = c(predControl, predTreatment), names_to = "tx_group", values_to = "pred")

grouped <- pred_long %>%
  group_by(model, tx_group) %>%
  group_split()

group_keys <- pred_long %>%
  group_by(model, tx_group) %>%
  group_keys()

results <- purrr::map(grouped, ~
  make_raster_map(.x, proj_crs, global_crs, "pred")
)

names(results) <- paste(group_keys$model, group_keys$tx_group, sep = "__")

raster_df <- imap_dfr(results, function(res, name) {
  
  # parse names like "gen_krige__Treatment"
  model <- strsplit(name, "__")[[1]][1]
  tx_group <- strsplit(name, "__")[[1]][2]
  
  as.data.frame(res, xy = TRUE, na.rm = FALSE) %>%
    mutate(
      model = model,
      tx_group = tx_group
    )
})

raster_df$model <- factor(raster_df$model, 
levels = c("simp_krig", "gen_krig", "gen_krig_int", "gen_krig_re"),
labels = c("Simple", "Gen", "Gen + int", "Gen + RE"),
ordered = TRUE)

raster_df$tx_group <- factor(raster_df$tx_group,
levels = c("predTreatment", "predControl"),
labels = c("Treatment", "Control"),
ordered = TRUE)

ggplot() +
  geom_raster(data = raster_df, aes(x = x, y = y, fill = pred), na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_sf(data = niger_adm2, fill = NA, color = "black", linewidth = 0.25) +
  facet_grid(tx_group ~ model) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  annotation_scale() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
  axis.title = element_blank()) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(limits = c(0, 35),
                      na.value = NA,
                      breaks = seq(0,30,by=10),
                      guide=guide_colorbar(title="Modeled mortality rate (per 1000 person-years)", 
                                          title.position = "top",
                                          title.hjust = 0.5,
                                          label.position = "bottom",
                                          label.hjust = 0.5,
                                          barheight=unit(10,"pt"),
                                          barwidth=unit(200,"pt"),
                                          ticks.colour = "white",
                                          ticks.linewidth = 1,
                                          frame.colour = "white")) +
  scale_y_continuous(n.breaks = 5) +
  scale_x_continuous(n.breaks = 3)

ggsave(here("results", "figs", "model_mort_pred.png"),
bg = "white",
width = 8, height = 6, units = "in")

```

The predicted mortality surfaces are visually similar across models, with consistent large-scale spatial patterns and only subtle differences in local variation (evidenced in the scatter plots below). This suggests that the larger spatial signal is captured even by simpler generalized kriging models.

```{r compare predictions}
pred_model_wide <- pred_long %>%
  dplyr::select(c(model, pred, tx_group, geometry)) %>%
  # mutate(row_n = row_number()) %>%
  pivot_wider(id_cols = c(tx_group, geometry), names_from = model, values_from = pred)

simp_corr_plot <- ggplot(data = pred_model_wide, aes(x = gen_krig, y = simp_krig, group = tx_group, color = tx_group)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3) +
  stat_cor(show.legend = FALSE) +
  theme_minimal() +
  scale_color_manual(breaks = c("predControl", "predTreatment"),
                    labels = c("Control", "Treatment"),
                     values = c("#fecd6c", "#e84d60"),
                     name = "Treatment Group") 

gen_int_corr_plot <- ggplot(data = pred_model_wide, aes(x = gen_krig, y = gen_krig_int, group = tx_group, color = tx_group)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3) +
  stat_cor(show.legend = FALSE) +
  theme_minimal() +
  scale_color_manual(breaks = c("predControl", "predTreatment"),
                    labels = c("Control", "Treatment"),
                     values = c("#fecd6c", "#e84d60"),
                     name = "Treatment Group") 

gen_re_corr_plot <- ggplot(data = pred_model_wide, aes(x = gen_krig, y = gen_krig_re, group = tx_group, color = tx_group)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3) +
  stat_cor(show.legend = FALSE) +
  theme_minimal() +
  scale_color_manual(breaks = c("predControl", "predTreatment"),
                    labels = c("Control", "Treatment"),
                     values = c("#fecd6c", "#e84d60"),
                     name = "Treatment Group") 

simp_corr_plot + gen_int_corr_plot + gen_re_corr_plot +
  plot_layout(guides = "collect") &
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

```

The high correlations between model predictions confirm that all models produce very similar estimates across the spatial domain. The simple kriging model shows slightly more deviation, consistent with its longer-range correlation structure and lack of covariates. The generalized models are nearly indistinguishable in their predictions, indicating that additional model complexity yields only marginal changes in fitted values.

## ATE estimates from spatial model predictions

```{r}
#| label: model-ate-maps
#| fig.width: 10
#| fig.height: 6

ate_long <- ate_preds %>%
  dplyr::select(-c(predControl, predTreatment))

grouped_ate <- ate_long %>%
  group_by(model) %>%
  group_split()

ate_group_keys <- ate_long %>%
  group_by(model) %>%
  group_keys()

ate_results <- purrr::map(grouped_ate, ~
  make_raster_map(.x, proj_crs, global_crs, "ATE")
)

names(ate_results) <- ate_group_keys$model
ate_raster_df <- imap_dfr(ate_results, function(res, name) {
  
  model <- name
  
  as.data.frame(res, xy = TRUE, na.rm = FALSE) %>%
    mutate(
      model = model
    )
})

ate_raster_df$model <- factor(ate_raster_df$model, 
levels = c("simp_krig", "gen_krig", "gen_krig_int", "gen_krig_re"),
labels = c("Simple", "Gen", "Gen + int", "Gen + RE"),
ordered = TRUE)

ggplot() +
  geom_raster(data = ate_raster_df, aes(x = x, y = y, fill = ATE), na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_sf(data = niger_adm2, fill = NA, color = "black", linewidth = 0.25) +
  facet_wrap(~ model, nrow = 1) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  annotation_scale() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
  axis.title = element_blank()) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = muted("dodgerblue"), 
                        mid = "white", 
                        high = muted("red"), 
                        midpoint = 0, 
                        limits = c(-13, 3),
                        na.value = NA,
                        breaks = seq(-10, 0, by = 5),
                        guide=guide_colorbar(title="ATE: difference in mortality rate (per 1000 person-years)", 
                                          title.position = "top",
                                          title.hjust = 0.5,
                                          label.position = "bottom",
                                          label.hjust = 0.5,
                                          barheight=unit(10,"pt"),
                                          barwidth=unit(200,"pt"),
                                          ticks.colour = "white",
                                          ticks.linewidth = 1,
                                          frame.colour = "white")) +
  scale_y_continuous(n.breaks = 5) +
  scale_x_continuous(n.breaks = 3)

ggsave(here("results", "figs", "model_ATE_map.png"),
bg = "white",
width = 8, height = 6, units = "in")

```

The generalized kriging model with interaction is the only model that clearly captures a localized positive ATE in Boboye. This suggests that allowing the treatment effect to vary with spatial covariates (latitude/longitude) is necessary to detect region-specific reversals in effect direction. There's also a possibility that the mordor model captures this too: need to check its predictions.

## Posterior probability OF ATE \< 0

```{r}
#| label: model-posterior-prob
#| fig.height: 6
#| fig.width: 8

post_prob <- post_prob_raw %>%
  dplyr::select(-c(neg_ate, total_ate))

grouped_post <- post_prob %>%
  group_by(model) %>%
  group_split()

post_group_keys <- post_prob %>%
  group_by(model) %>%
  group_keys()

post_results <- purrr::map(grouped_post, ~
  make_raster_map(.x, proj_crs, global_crs, "prob")
)

names(post_results) <- post_group_keys$model
post_raster_df <- imap_dfr(post_results, function(res, name) {
  
  model <- name
  
  as.data.frame(res, xy = TRUE, na.rm = FALSE) %>%
    mutate(
      model = model
    )
})

post_raster_df$model <- factor(post_raster_df$model, 
levels = c("gen_krig", "gen_krig_int"),
labels = c("Gen", "Gen + int"),
ordered = TRUE)

ggplot() +
  geom_raster(data = post_raster_df, aes(x = x, y = y, fill = prob), na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_sf(data = niger_adm2, fill = NA, color = "black", linewidth = 0.25) +
  facet_wrap(~ model, nrow = 1) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  annotation_scale() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
  axis.title = element_blank()) +
  scale_fill_viridis(option = "magma", direction = 1,
                      limits = c(0.3, 1),
                      na.value = NA,
                      # breaks = seq(0,10,by=2),
                      guide = guide_colorbar(title="Posterior pr(mortality ATE < 0)",  
                                          title.position = "top",
                                          title.hjust = 0.5,
                                          label.position = "bottom",
                                          label.hjust = 0.5,
                                          barheight=unit(10,"pt"),
                                          barwidth=unit(200,"pt"),
                                          ticks.colour = "white",
                                          ticks.linewidth = 1,
                                          frame.colour = "white")) +
  scale_y_continuous(n.breaks = 5) +
  scale_x_continuous(n.breaks = 3)

ggsave(here("results", "figs", "model_posterior_prob_map.png"),
bg = "white",
width = 8, height = 6, units = "in")

```


The posterior probability map provides a probabilistic interpretation of treatment benefit. Areas with high probability (close to 1) indicate strong evidence that treatment reduces mortality, while lower values indicate uncertainty or potential harm. Compared to the base generalized model, the interaction model produces more spatially differentiated probability surfaces, particularly in regions like Boboye, where the probability of benefit is substantially lower. This reinforces the conclusion that treatment effects are spatially heterogeneous.

This was estimated using a simulation-based approach where we drew samples from the posterior distribution of model parameters, calculated the ATE for each sample, and then computed the proportion of samples where the ATE was less than 0 at each location. This approach accounts for uncertainty in model parameters and provides a more nuanced assessment of treatment effects across space.

# CSI-level analysis

We also fit spatial models at the CSI level, which has less spatial granularity than the grappe-level data but may still capture some spatial correlation. Since the randomization was at the grappe level, we cannot include a term for the treatment indicator in the CSI-level models, but we can still fit spatial models to predict mortality rates across the study area and compare the spatial correlation structure to the grappe-level models, akin to how it will be done in future programmatic surveillance analyses.

![](images/matern_corrs_csi.png)

```{r}
#| label: csi-model-predictions
#| fig.height: 6
#| fig.width: 8

csi_preds_long <- csi_preds %>%
  dplyr::select(-c(isTreated_child))

grouped_csi_preds <- csi_preds_long %>%
  group_by(model) %>%
  group_split()

csi_group_keys <- csi_preds_long %>%
  group_by(model) %>%
  group_keys()

csi_results <- purrr::map(grouped_csi_preds, ~
  make_raster_map(.x, proj_crs, global_crs, "pred")
)

names(csi_results) <- csi_group_keys$model
csi_raster_df <- imap_dfr(csi_results, function(res, name) {
  
  model <- name
  
  as.data.frame(res, xy = TRUE, na.rm = FALSE) %>%
    mutate(
      model = model
    )
})

csi_raster_df$model <- factor(csi_raster_df$model, 
levels = c("simp_krig", "gen_krig"),
labels = c("Simple", "Gen"),
ordered = TRUE)

ggplot() +
  geom_raster(data = csi_raster_df, aes(x = x, y = y, fill = pred), na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_sf(data = niger_adm2_sub, fill = NA, color = "black", linewidth = 0.25) +
  facet_wrap(~ model, nrow = 1) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  annotation_scale() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
  axis.title = element_blank()) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(limits = c(0, 35),
                      na.value = NA,
                      breaks = seq(0,30,by=10),
                      guide=guide_colorbar(title="Modeled mortality rate (per 1000 person-years)", 
                                          title.position = "top",
                                          title.hjust = 0.5,
                                          label.position = "bottom",
                                          label.hjust = 0.5,
                                          barheight=unit(10,"pt"),
                                          barwidth=unit(200,"pt"),
                                          ticks.colour = "white",
                                          ticks.linewidth = 1,
                                          frame.colour = "white")) +
  scale_y_continuous(n.breaks = 5) +
  scale_x_continuous(n.breaks = 3)

ggsave(here("results", "figs", "csi_model_mort_pred.png"),
bg = "white",
width = 8, height = 6, units = "in")

```

When comparing this csi-level aggregate analysis to the grappe-level analysis, we see that the csi-level models have a larger Matern correlation range (14.38 km for the generalized kriging model) compared to the grappe-level models (range of 11.27 km for the generalized kriging model and 11.37 km when we include an interaction with treatment). This suggests that there is more spatial correlation in the grappe-level data than in the csi-level data, which makes sense given that the grappe-level data has more spatial granularity and may capture more local spatial patterns.

Despite the loss of spatial resolution, the CSI-level analysis preserves the broad spatial gradients in mortality. However, the increased correlation range suggests that aggregation smooths over local variability, effectively inflating the apparent spatial scale of dependence. This implies that CSI-level surveillance may be adequate for identifying large-scale patterns but may miss localized hotspots or heterogeneity in treatment effects that are detectable at the grappe level.



# Variance partitioning

Using a model with treatment indicator, matern correlation, and a random effect for district and csi nested in district, we partition the variance in mortality rates (on the latent scale) into components attributable to treatment, spatial correlation (sub-csi level variance), district-level effects, and csi-level effects.

The variance partitioning results suggest that approximately 97.6% of the variance in mortality is explained by fine-scale spatial correlation, 2.4% is explained by differences between CSIs within districts, and 0% is explained by differences between districts.
